beats.text: PEMDAS is just a string of initials.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says

beats.text: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication, Division, Addition, Subtraction.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says

beats.text: In Britain they call it BODMAS, in Canada BEDMAS. The letters change a little from country to country, but the idea stays the same.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says

beats.text: Here is where many people go astray.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: You see the M before the D, and it is easy to think that multiplication always comes before division.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: You see the A before the S, and it is easy to think that addition always comes before subtraction.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: But that is not the rule.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: Multiplication and division sit on the same level, and you work through them from left to right, whichever comes first.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: Addition and subtraction share a level too, and they also go from left to right.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: Take ten minus three plus two.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: If you believe addition has to come first, you work out three plus two, which is five, and then ten minus five, which is five.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: But read it from left to right, the way the rule really says. Ten minus three is seven, and seven plus two is nine.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: The answer is nine.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: Or take eight divided by four, times two.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: Left to right, eight divided by four is two, and two times two is four.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: Do the multiplication first, because the M comes before the D, and you get four times two is eight, then eight divided by eight is one. Wrong again.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: I start here because it matters.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: A large share of those online fights happen simply because people misremember the levels.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: Once you know that multiplication and division are equals, and addition and subtraction are equals, a lot of the famous arguments quietly disappear.
beats.act: ACT ONE — What PEMDAS really says
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: So which parts of PEMDAS did people simply decide, with nothing in nature forcing them?
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice
beats.section: The part almost everyone gets wrong

beats.text: The first is reading from left to right.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: When two operations sit on the same level, like addition and subtraction, we agree to do the left one first. But that is purely a choice.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: Arabic is written from right to left, and in principle we could just as well have agreed to read our sums in that direction.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: In fact, someone did. In the nineteen sixties, a programming language called APL was built to read every expression from right to left, with no ladder of priorities at all.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: And even in ordinary maths, we already break our own habit. Two to the three to the two, a tower of powers, is worked out from the top down. It comes to five hundred and twelve, not sixty-four.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: No law of nature says an expression must be read from left to right.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: The second point, and I think the most important one, is the role of brackets.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: Brackets always win.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: Want to add before you multiply? Just put the addition in brackets, and you're done.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: Which means PEMDAS is really the rule for when we get lazy, for when we leave the brackets out to keep things short.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: If you always wrote every bracket, PEMDAS would be almost useless, because the brackets would already tell you what to do first.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: In other words, PEMDAS is a rule about how we write and read. It is not a property of the numbers themselves.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: The third clue is the name itself.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: PEMDAS, BODMAS, BEDMAS, a different one in every country.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: The very fact that one rule goes by so many names tells you it is the product of an agreement.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: It's like choosing which side of the road to drive on.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: Everyone needs a shared rule, but the particular rule could have been different, and the world would still work.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: As for when it happened, the history is less tidy than you might expect.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: Putting multiplication before addition grew up with algebra itself, in the sixteen hundreds, as mathematicians started writing equations in symbols.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: But the full rule, spelled out in schoolbooks, only settled in around the late eighteen hundreds and early nineteen hundreds, as algebra and printed textbooks spread.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: And it did not settle quietly. In nineteen seventeen, an American maths journal was already debating whether multiplication should go before division.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: The catchy names, like PEMDAS, came later still. The rule grew up with our need to write mathematics briefly, and all in the same way.
beats.act: ACT TWO — The part that really is just a choice

beats.text: If we stopped at "it's just a convention", we would be a little unfair to PEMDAS.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: Because out of all the rules we could have picked, the one humanity settled on is a very clever one.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: Think about why multiplication outranks addition.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: The reason is polynomials, the things you write all the time in algebra. Take three x squared, plus two x, plus one.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: With multiplication before addition, you can write that with no brackets at all. It is clean, and easy to read.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: If addition outranked multiplication, you would need brackets everywhere just to say the same thing.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: Three x squared in brackets, plus two x in brackets, plus one. Tiring just to look at.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: There is a deeper reason too, called the distributive law.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: When you write a times the bracket b plus c, it equals a b plus a c.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: Giving multiplication the higher priority fits that law perfectly. The way we write things down mirrors the way the operations actually behave.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: And why do powers sit above multiplication? Picture a ladder.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: Multiplication is, at heart, repeated addition. Three times four is four, added three times.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: A power is repeated multiplication. Four cubed is four, multiplied by itself three times.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: On that ladder, the stronger the operation, the higher it sits, and the earlier it is done. It binds more tightly to the numbers around it.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: Powers above multiplication, multiplication above addition.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: The ladder is one way to see why the convention we chose feels so natural, and holds together so well.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: So I think the fairest way to put it is this.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: Out of all the conventions we could have invented, PEMDAS is close to the one that lets us write the most common expressions with the fewest brackets.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: It is tuned for the things people write most, and that is why it feels natural.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: But that natural feeling comes from convenience. Not from an unbreakable truth of mathematics.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Not an arbitrary choice

beats.text: Now let's go back to the sum from the start. Six divided by two, times the bracket one plus two.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: Do the bracket first. One plus two is three, which leaves six divided by two, times three.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: Multiplication and division are on the same level, so go from left to right.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: Six divided by two is three, and three times three is nine. Nine.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: But the people who say one have a point as well.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: They look at that two pressed right up against the bracket, a multiplication with no sign, just a number touching a bracket.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: In a lot of handwritten maths, especially in physics and engineering, this kind of glued-on multiplication is quietly treated as stronger than an ordinary division sign.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: Read that way, two times three comes first, which is six, and six divided by six is one. One.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: Even calculators can't agree.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: Older Texas Instruments models gave that glued-on multiplication the higher priority. Later models treat it like any other multiplication.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: Same company, same keys, different answers.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: When the people who build calculators can't agree with each other, you know the problem is not about who is smarter.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: The most honest answer to this sum is that it is badly written. It is ambiguous.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: A good expression should never make its reader guess.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: In practice, mathematicians almost never write it this way. They use a fraction bar.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: Six on top and two times three underneath, or six over two, then times three, whichever they mean, and the argument is over.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: That little division sign, a dot above and a dot below a line, has been fading out of serious mathematics for a long time. International standards for scientific writing even advise against using it.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: And this is the point I want to underline.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: If PEMDAS were an unbreakable truth of mathematics, there could be no expression where two people follow the rule correctly and get two different answers.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: The fact that such expressions exist shows that the rule has gaps.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — Where the convention runs out

beats.text: There is one small example I love, because it says everything.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: In the usual mathematical convention, minus two squared means: square the two first, then attach the minus sign. So the answer is minus four.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: But type exactly the same thing into Excel, and Excel gives you plus four.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: Because Excel was built so that the minus sign holds on tighter than the power. It takes minus two first, and then squares it.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: Python, on the other hand, says minus four.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: And JavaScript refuses to answer at all. It stops with an error, and asks you to add brackets.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: Same expression, different systems, different answers, all because each one ranks the operations its own way.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: If the order of operations were an unbreakable truth of mathematics, the people who built these programs could not have chosen differently.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: So here is my answer to the question in the title.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: PEMDAS is simply how we agreed to read and write mathematics briefly.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: It is a shortcut. Brackets are the real tool.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: And the lesson is a simple one.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: When you write an expression that someone could misread, don't trust that everybody remembers PEMDAS the same way. Just add the brackets.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: A good expression is one its reader never has to argue about.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.text: Thank you for watching all the way to the end.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?

beats.act: ACT FIVE — So, natural, or agreed?
